Solar Manufacturing: 90% Localised by 2030
India’s solar story is increasingly moving beyond installation and into manufacturing.

According to Jefferies’ recent India’s New Industrial Revolution report, India is already the world’s second-largest solar PV manufacturing base, with around 35 GW of cell capacity operational and another ~100 GW under construction. Solar generation capacity has also crossed 150 GW as of March 2026.

The bigger opportunity, however, is localisation. With the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), domestic-content requirements and the PLI scheme supporting the ecosystem, India could reach nearly 90% localisation of solar manufacturing by 2030.

And this creates an interesting second-order opportunity: the electronics behind the solar ecosystem.

Solar inverters, charge controllers, energy-management systems and smart-grid electronics require increasingly sophisticated PCB assemblies. 
As India builds a more localised solar supply chain, these high-value electronics could become an emerging opportunity for EMS players.

The solar opportunity, therefore, may not just be about panels and cells. The entire manufacturing ecosystem around solar is getting built in India.

Steel Exchange India Limited | Entering a Stronger Steel Demand & Pricing Cycle 🏭📈

Indian steel prices are gaining momentum as post-monsoon infrastructure and automotive demand improves. HRC prices have risen by ~₹4,000/tonne between August and early September, while another ~₹3,500/tonne increase is expected in the coming weeks. Tighter spot availability, lean distributor inventories, planned maintenance shutdowns and higher coking coal costs are supporting the price recovery.

What makes this particularly relevant for Steel Exchange India Limited is that the company is entering this period with higher Re-Bar production capability and a new long-term raw material sourcing arrangement.

🔹 SEIL achieved its highest-ever monthly Re-Bar production of 24,823.509 MT in August 2026, with the newly operationalised RHF contributing 7,465.288 MT.

🔹 The RHF has increased monthly Re-Bar production capability by ~27%, with the company looking to sustain higher production levels going forward.

🔹 SEIL has signed a 4-year MoU with NMDC Limited for the supply and procurement of consistent-grade Iron Ore Fines (Fe 61–63% and above) from the upcoming Visakhapatnam Buffer Hub.

🔹 The proximity of the hub to SEIL’s facilities could provide lower freight costs and minimal transit times, while improving raw material supply visibility.

The interesting part: The company is adding production capability at a time when steel demand and prices are showing improvement, while the NMDC arrangement adds greater visibility on a key raw material.

Higher infrastructure demand → Re-Bar demand | RHF → higher production capability | NMDC MoU → consistent-grade iron ore | Nearby hub → logistics benefits

This combination could help SEIL improve capacity utilisation and benefit from the improving steel market as production ramps up.

Adisoft Technologies Limited | Riding India’s Automation & Robotics Build-Out 🤖🏭

India’s manufacturing sector is moving deeper into automation, robotics and smart factories. Invest India highlights the growing adoption of AI, IoT and digitally connected manufacturing, while IFR data shows India installed a record 9,120 industrial robots in 2024 — up 7% YoY and ranking 6th globally.

What makes this particularly interesting for Adisoft is that the company operates directly at the intersection of these trends — robotics, factory automation and shop-floor digitalisation.

🔹 1,000+ installations and 950+ customers served, with turnkey capabilities spanning automated assembly lines, robotic cells, SPMs, vision systems, material handling and IoT.

🔹 Automotive — one of the biggest adopters of robotics — contributes ~64% of Adisoft’s FY26 revenue, with solutions deployed across assembly, weld, paint and engine lines.

🔹 Adisoft goes beyond standalone machines — its key differentiation is connecting shop-floor equipment with IT/ERP and MES, enabling real-time monitoring, traceability and Industry 4.0 manufacturing.

🔹 Its portfolio is moving towards higher-value smart-factory solutions such as AI vision inspection, robotics, traceability and poka-yoke — areas where the company says it is seeing its strongest demand.

🔹 And capacity is being built for the opportunity: Adisoft’s new 70,000 sq ft Pune facility carries management-indicated peak revenue potential of ₹650–700 Cr over ~5 years, versus FY26 revenue of ~₹166 Cr.

The interesting part: India is still scaling up factory automation, while Adisoft already has the customer base, automotive presence, engineering capability and smart-factory stack to participate in that transition.

More robots → more integration | Smarter factories → more digitalisation | Industry 4.0 → IT-to-shop-floor connectivity | Manufacturing expansion → more automation opportunities

TEGA INDUSTRIES | MOLYCOP CHANGED THE SCALE — NOT YET THE ECONOMICS

Q1 consolidated revenue reached ₹1,720 Cr, but includes only one month of Molycop. It is therefore not a steady quarterly run-rate.

The useful disaggregation:

• Legacy Tega: ₹430 Cr revenue, +21%; EBITDA margin 22.1%.
• Legacy consumables: ₹400 Cr revenue, +36%; margin 24.1%.
• Molycop: ₹1,290 Cr revenue; ₹160 Cr EBITDA; margin ~13%.
• Net debt: ₹6,366 Cr, down ₹3,218 Cr from March.
• Provisional goodwill: ~₹5,000 Cr.
• Synergy target: ~$20 million over 2–2.5 years.

Patrick Koley: “The majority of our customer contracts are tied to steel indices… it protects our gross margin.”

Mehul Mohanka: “The combined platform is well positioned to capitalize on attractive growth opportunities across the mining value chain.”

Ravi Joshi: “This quarter includes only one month consolidation of Molycop performance. It would be premature to draw conclusions regarding the full-year outlook…”

Margin protection → Cross-selling → Synergy → Debt reduction

Revenue scale alone proves none of these.

WATCH

• Molycop margin
• Q3/Q4 cross-selling
• Net-debt reduction

KEY RISK

Integration costs, weaker mining throughput or leverage absorbing the synergy.

DISC: Not a recommendation

Festive Travel Surge Could Support Praveg Limited’s Expanding Luxury Resort Portfolio

India’s festive travel season is building early, with travellers planning longer holidays and spending more on premium stays and experiences, a trend closely aligned with Praveg Limited’s experiential luxury resort portfolio across beach, island, spiritual and nature-led destinations.

- Leisure hotel bookings are running ~10–15% ahead YoY
- Room rates at high-demand leisure hotels are ~8–10% higher YoY
- Festive travel searches have jumped ~40–45% MoM
- Travellers are increasingly choosing 5–9 day itineraries and spending more on experiences

Praveg Limited enters this demand cycle at a much larger scale, with 17 resorts and 827+ rooms. The company sold 1.21 lakh rooms in FY26, up from 88,426 in FY25, while another 577 rooms are planned across upcoming destinations.

With higher festive occupancy, stronger room rates and rising preference for experience-led holidays, the upcoming festive and wedding season could provide a favourable demand environment for Praveg Limited’s growing luxury hospitality portfolio.

MONOLITHISCH INDIA: SECURES 35.5 LAKH MT QUARTZITE BLOCK IN BIHAR; COMPLETES BACKWARD INTEGRATION

• Company secured a Quartzite Stone Block in Nawada, Bihar through a government e-auction at a winning bid of ₹157 crore for 5 years.
• Approved mining capacity stands at 7.10 lakh MT per annum, aggregating 35.50 lakh MT over the 5-year lease period.
• Captive quartzite supply will strengthen raw-material security and hedge input costs as the group expands silica ramming-mass capacity to ~5.76 lakh MTPA.
• Statutory approvals are expected within 3–4 months, with commercial mining targeted from February/March 2027.
• Management expects raw-material procurement costs to fall significantly once mining commences and inventory requirements to reduce substantially.
• Mining will be executed through per-ton raising contracts, limiting direct infrastructure capex.
• Company plans a beneficiation and storage facility near the mine to improve quality consistency and support development of new products.
• Management also targets a 50% reduction in raw-material inventory in H2 FY27, supporting its goal of a near debt-free balance sheet.

Impact: Positive — Large captive quartzite resource completes backward integration, improves raw-material security and has potential to materially reduce costs and strengthen margins.

RAGHAV PRODUCTIVITY ENHANCERS: UNVEILS ‘RPEL 2.0’ 2031 STRATEGY; TARGETS 1 MN MT RAW-MATERIAL CAPACITY & HIGH-VALUE SILICA PRODUCTS

• Company outlined 5 growth engines through 2031 — Nippon Steel-group JV, multi-location manufacturing, global foundries, Electric Arc Furnace products and moving up the high-purity silica value chain.

• 80:20 JV with TRL Krosaki Refractories, a Nippon Steel subsidiary, will establish capacity in East India; RPEL will also receive royalty for its manufacturing technology.

• JV is expected to unlock around 3.5 lakh MTPA capacity closer to a major demand cluster and potentially reduce outward freight from ₹2,500–3,500/MT to ₹500–700/MT.

• Multi-location manufacturing strategy targets 1 million MT raw-material capacity, aimed at lowering freight, inventory and lead times while accelerating market-share gains.

• Company is targeting the 50,000+ global foundry market; foundry products can command around 3x higher realization than conventional steel-grade ramming mass.

• RPEL is expanding into Tundish Mass for Electric Arc Furnaces, a higher-margin product which it says offers around 10x the life of traditional tundish boards.

• High-purity silica strategy could materially increase realization: current ramming-mass products are around ₹7,000–25,000/tonne, while aspirational 6N semiconductor-grade quartz can reach ~₹6.5–7 lakh/tonne.

• Over FY16–FY26, RPEL says volumes increased from 29 KMT to 332 KMT (12x) and PAT from around ₹1 crore to ₹55 crore (55x); EBITDA/tonne improved from ~₹1,245 to ~₹2,650.

Impact: Positive — RPEL 2.0 targets major capacity expansion, lower logistics costs and a shift toward substantially higher-value products, potentially supporting stronger margins and a much larger addressable market through 2031.

Copper Is Sending a Very Different Message Than Oil

Why Copper Crashed

Copper’s drop today needs to be separated into the immediate trigger and the macro backdrop.

The immediate trigger was Washington. Traders had built a tariff premium into copper because they expected the White House to extend duties to refined copper. That helped pull metal into the U.S. and push prices higher.

When reports surfaced that the decision had stalled over affordability concerns, that premium unwound violently. Copper fell more than 4%.

Washington pulled the trigger. The macro environment determines what happens next.

The $100 Oil Problem

Brent is above $100 while the dollar is strengthening and financial conditions are tightening.

Higher oil creates two opposing forces.

•    Mining and transportation become more expensive
•    Industrial demand weakens as energy costs squeeze consumers and businesses

Eventually the second can dominate.

Higher production costs cannot guarantee higher copper prices if factories stop buying.

Energy inflation raises freight and manufacturing costs, compresses margins and reduces household purchasing power. It also keeps central banks cautious, real rates higher and the dollar stronger.

That pressures construction, manufacturing and autos.

Oil can rise because supply has disappeared while copper falls because markets fear demand disappears next.

Gold and Silver Add Another Signal

Copper was not alone. Gold and silver also sold off sharply after the 5.4% PPI reading while Treasury yields and the dollar moved higher.

Gold can fall when hotter inflation pushes real yields higher. Silver also carries industrial exposure, making it vulnerable when higher rates collide with weaker growth.

Copper, gold and silver falling together while oil surges does not look like a broad commodity boom. It looks more like an energy shock tightening financial conditions.

History Shows Two Oil Regimes

When oil rises because global growth is booming, copper often rises with it. That happened during the 2007 to 2008 commodity boom.

Supply shocks behave differently. In 2022 Brent surged above $100 and copper initially hit record highs. But as tightening intensified, China weakened and recession fears grew, copper later lost roughly a third of its value.

Demand driven $100 oil can coexist with rising copper. Supply driven $100 oil in restrictive financial conditions is far more dangerous.

What Matters Next

Copper still has a powerful long term story from grids, electrification, defense spending and AI. That does not prevent a severe cyclical decline.

Today’s copper crash alone does not prove recession. The tariff reversal accelerated it.

But if Brent stays above $100 while copper keeps weakening, precious metals stay pressured, the dollar strengthens and global cyclicals roll over, the message becomes harder to dismiss.

Oil and copper rising together usually signal strong nominal global activity.

Oil rising while copper falls can signal scarcity in energy colliding with weakening demand elsewhere.

Today we are beginning to see the latter.

KSH INTERNATIONAL | SUPA CAPACITY RAMP-UP

A small regulatory approval that could unlock a much bigger capacity ramp.

KSH International has received the Consent to Operate (CTO) from the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board for its Supa facility in Maharashtra.

The Supa facility manufactures specialised and standard magnet winding wires — critical components used in electrical equipment and power applications.

With the CTO now in place, the approved manufacturing capacity at Supa stands at 28,800 MTPA.

That makes the approval more than just a regulatory checkbox. It potentially allows the company to move towards commercial utilisation of a significantly larger manufacturing base, subject to execution and customer demand.

KEY THINGS TO WATCH
→ Capacity utilisation
→ Customer additions and order inflow
→ Mix between specialised vs standard winding wires
→ Revenue and margin contribution from Supa
→ Return on capital deployed

The more interesting part is that specialised winding wires can carry higher value-add than commoditised products. So, the quality of capacity utilisation could matter just as much as the quantity.

The CTO is valid until August 31, 2027.

KEY TAKEAWAY
For investors, this is an execution trigger rather than an earnings trigger today.

The next step is to see the approval translate into:

Production → Utilisation → Revenue → Earnings

The real value creation will depend on how quickly KSH International converts the newly enabled capacity into high-quality revenue and sustainable returns.

Coforge Chairman resignation : Lets dig deeper

OP Bhatt's resignation came after disagreements around the Board evaluation process. In his resignation note, he says continuing on Board amid differences regarding his "good faith actions" would not be conducive to Board effective functioning 

OP Bhatt is not a conventional IT industry chairman. He is among India's most respected bankers, having led SBI between 2006-11 & later served on boards across large corporates including Tata Group companies

The market doesn’t take such update kindly, but Bhatt's continuation was already under question even before the resignation. Shareholders (inc largest shareholder Advent) voted against his reappointment as Independent Director from May'27
 
Let’s go a bit in history: The company was earlier known as NIIT Tech before its ownership transition & eventual rebranding to Coforge. Barings acquired control of NIIT in 2020, leading to ownership change then.

Later, Barings steadily monetised its stake through multiple block deals as the company scaled in size, profitability & market value. After Barings' complete exit by FY24, Co. become fully public market institutional owned.

OP Bhatt joined the board in 2024 & became Chairman during a phase when Coforge was pursuing aggressive scale-up ambitions. Coforge accelerated inorganic growth. The acquisition of Cigniti significantly expanded its engineering & digital capabilities under him.

The much bigger acquisition Encora was also under OP Bhatt. The acquisition materially increased Coforge's scale, global delivery footprint & exposure to high-growth digital engineering segments.

Encora also changed the shareholding landscape. Through the transaction, Advent became the largest shareholder in Coforge, making its views impossible for the board to ignore. That's why the key takeaway may not be the resignation itself. The bigger story could be that the largest shareholder & the Chairman were not aligned on important matters. 

The bullish view is that management execution remains intact. The cautious view is that whenever Chairman, Board & largest shareholder are not on the same page, governance questions emerge and mgmt. energy is focussed away from growth.

• Devyani’s Board had approved the amended merger scheme on August 26, 2026.
• The CCI filing is part of the required regulatory approval process for completing the merger.
• Transaction remains subject to necessary regulatory and other approvals.

Impact: Positive — Progress on CCI approval moves the merger closer to completion and can strengthen Devyani’s scale and QSR market presence.

MEESHO, NYKAA – NEW E-COMMERCE RULES

Key Changes
- Rules effective January 1, 2027
- Sponsored listings need clear disclosure
- Search results cannot be misleadingly manipulated
- 30-day lowest price must be displayed
- Annual dark-pattern audits become mandatory
- Clear seller and refund details required
- Express consent needed for specified data use
- National Consumer Helpline integration required

Key Takeaway
- Higher transparency and compliance requirements
- Could impact platform operating practices

What connects all six sectors?

India is gradually moving through the same industrial ladder:

Imports → Assembly → Components → Technology → Full value-chain localisation → Exports

🔹Space is moving private.
🔹Semiconductors are moving from policy to production.

🔹Electronics is moving beyond assembly.
🔹Solar is moving upstream.
🔹Aerospace is entering global supply chains.

Source: Jefferies Equity Research, “India’s New Industrial Revolution”, September 8, 2026.

6️⃣AEROSPACE: Global Demand, Global Bottleneck

Aerospace is entering a long demand cycle.

Airbus expects the global passenger fleet to rise from roughly:

23,000 aircraft in 2025 → 46,000 by 2045.

Around 42,000 new aircraft could be required over the period.

But production capacity cannot easily keep up.

The global aerospace backlog exceeds 17,000 aircraft, roughly 12 years of current production capacity.

Engines, forgings, castings and precision components remain major bottlenecks.

That supply constraint is creating space for new manufacturing geographies.

Including India.

India Is Already Entering Global Aircraft Programs

India’s aircraft/spacecraft/components exports rose from roughly:

$1.4 Bn FY20 → $7 Bn FY25.

Boeing already sources $1.4 Bn+ annually from 375+ Indian suppliers.

Airbus sources roughly $1.6 Bn annually and targets ~$2 Bn before 2030.

Solar’s Real Moat Could Move Upstream

Module manufacturing is becoming crowded.

The tougher part is backward integration.

Jefferies estimates roughly:
Cell capex: ~$70 Mn/GW
Ingot/wafer capex: broadly similar
Integrated ingot-to-cell: ~$140 Mn/GW

That requires capital, technology and execution capability.

Jefferies expects cell supply-demand to balance earlier, while wafer/ingot shortages could persist longer.

Meaning pricing power may shift towards the handful of genuinely integrated manufacturers.

By 2030, India could localise roughly 90% of the solar manufacturing value chain.

5️⃣SOLAR: India Is Already #2 Globally

India has emerged as the world's second-largest solar PV manufacturing base.

Current module capacity: around 156 GW

Current cell capacity: around 35 GW

Another 100 GW of cell capacity is under construction.

Roughly 60 GW of ingot/wafer capacity is also being developed.

The solar manufacturing story is therefore changing from:

Import cells → assemble modules → manufacture cells → manufacture wafers/ingots.

Solar + BESS Changes the Economics

One reason this manufacturing capacity may find demand:

Solar + storage is becoming competitive against new thermal generation.

Jefferies highlights recent solar + BESS economics of roughly:

₹4.5–5/kWh

versus marginal thermal generation around:

₹5.8–6.3/kWh

Solar+BESS contracts can also lock tariffs for long periods, while thermal costs can rise.

Jefferies projects annual solar additions moving from around 57 GWdc in FY26 → ~74 GWdc by FY30E.

4️⃣ELECTRONICS: Assembly Was Phase 1

India’s electronics production has more than doubled in five years:

₹5.5 Tn FY21 → ₹12.1 Tn FY26.

Electronics exports grew nearly 5x.

And smartphones became India's largest exported product category in FY26.

But there is one weakness:

India assembles phones domestically, yet a large portion of the components still comes from abroad.

So the next phase is not more assembly.

It is backward integration.

India Wants to Localise the Inside of the Phone

Roughly 99% of phones sold in India are now assembled domestically.

But domestic value addition remains relatively low.

The ECMS component scheme is targeting localisation across:

🔸 PCBs
🔸 Camera modules
🔸 Display modules
🔸 Enclosures
🔸 Li-ion cells
🔸 Copper laminates
🔸 Passive components
🔸 Optical transceivers

Jefferies forecasts ECMS could eventually cover roughly 50% of mobile-phone BoM, versus below 20% currently.

₹1.15 Trillion of Component Capex Applications

The response to ECMS has been significantly stronger than initially expected.

Initial capex target: ₹594 Bn

Applications/commitments: approximately ₹1,154 Bn

Nearly 2x the original target.

106 projects had already received approvals by Aug-26.

Listed companies involved include:
🔹Dixon: display/camera modules
🔹Syrma SGS: multilayer/HDI PCBs, camera modules, coils
🔹Kaynes: PCBs, copper laminates, camera modules

This is where EMS businesses increasingly become component manufacturing platforms.

Who Sells the Picks & Shovels?

Jefferies sees electrical infrastructure as one of the largest beneficiaries of the DC buildout.

Companies exposed across the ecosystem include:
🔹Power/T&D: Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova T&D, ABB, Siemens
🔹Gensets: Cummins India, Kirloskar Oil Engines
Cables: Polycab, KEI, Finolex
🔹Cooling: Blue Star, Voltas
🔹Operators/infra: Bharti Airtel, Anant Raj, Lodha and others

The key insight:
Data centers are basically giant power infrastructure projects with servers inside them.

The Bigger Data-Center Opportunity Is Outside the Data Center

Jefferies estimates $45 Bn of facility capex may be required over CY27–31.

Approximate split:
$16 Bn: Power & electrical systems
$11 Bn: Land/shell
$9 Bn: Racks/fit-outs
$7 Bn: Cooling
$2 Bn: Network infrastructure

Add $90 Bn of server capex and the total ecosystem funding requirement approaches $135 Bn.
That is why the data-center boom can spill into electrical equipment, cables, cooling, gensets, construction and telecom infrastructure.

3️⃣DATA CENTERS: Another 5x Expansion

India's colocation data-center capacity has already expanded roughly 5x over the past few years to ~2 GW.

Jefferies expects another:

2 GW today → 10 GW by 2031.

Why?
Cloud adoption
AI/compute demand
Digitisation
Data localisation
BFSI demand
Hyperscaler expansion

Current utilisation is already estimated at roughly 95–97%, meaning this isn't simply speculative capacity creation.

Semicon 2.0 Makes the Opportunity Much Bigger

India has now launched a second semiconductor incentive programme with roughly ₹1.28 Tn / $13 Bn of incentives.

It expands beyond fabs into:
🔹Semiconductor equipment
🔹Materials
🔹Specialty gases & chemicals
🔹Advanced packaging
🔹Chip design
🔹R&D
🔹Talent development
The government expects this phase to attract around $42 Bn of investment.

And India already accounts for roughly 20% of the world's semiconductor design workforce.

So the opportunity is increasingly moving from “manufacture chips in India” → “build the semiconductor ecosystem in India.”

2️⃣SEMICONDUCTORS: Policy Is Turning Into Factories

India's semiconductor story has moved beyond announcements.

Phase 1 of the semiconductor programme has triggered roughly $20 Bn of investments.

Projects now include:
🔸Tata Electronics semiconductor fab
🔸Tata Assam OSAT
🔸Micron ATMP
🔸CG Power OSAT
🔸Kaynes OSAT
🔸HCL-Foxconn OSAT
🔸SiC fabs
🔸Advanced packaging facilities

This is still early - but India is finally building multiple layers of the semiconductor ecosystem simultaneously.

India's Largest Chip Bet

Tata Electronics is constructing roughly an $11 Bn semiconductor fab in Gujarat with Taiwan’s PSMC.

Planned capacity: 50,000 12-inch wafers/month.

Target technologies: roughly 28–110nm.

That matters because India does not need to immediately beat TSMC at cutting-edge 2nm chips.

Huge demand still exists in mature nodes across:
🔹Automotive
🔹Industrial
🔹Telecom
🔹IoT
🔹Consumer electronics

India’s near-term semiconductor opportunity may be about commercial scale, not technological bragging rights.

The Space Startup Ecosystem Has Exploded

India had barely 1 space startup in 2014.

By 2026: 400+ startups.

Some names to understand:
🔹Skyroot: launch vehicles; Vikram-1
🔹Pixxel: hyperspectral Earth-observation satellites
🔹Agnikul:  single-piece 3D-printed semi-cryogenic rocket engine
🔹Digantara: space surveillance/orbital debris tracking
🔹Bellatrix: in-space propulsion
🔹Dhruva Space: satellites + ground infrastructure
🔹SatSure: satellite analytics

Private investment reached roughly $0.6 Bn by FY26.
India’s space story is moving from government missions → commercial ecosystem.

1️⃣SPACE: The ₹ Opportunity Is Moving Private

India has spent decades building end-to-end space capabilities through ISRO.

But the structural change came in 2020, when the space value chain was opened to private participation.

The government is targeting India's space economy to expand from roughly $8.4 Bn in 2023 → $40–45 Bn by 2030 → $100 Bn by 2040.

That is nearly a 5x opportunity this decade.

Why India Has an Edge in Space

India’s advantage is not simply lower labour costs.

It is frugal engineering.

ISRO's FY26 space budget was only around $1.4 Bn, versus NASA's $25 Bn FY25 budget.

Yet India has executed missions including Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan and 400 satellite launches for global customers over 2014–26.

Mangalyaan reportedly cost only ~$74 Mn, while Chandrayaan-3 cost roughly $72 Mn.

India has learned how to do highly complex engineering with dramatically less capital.

India Is Not Starting From Zero

The important point: India’s new manufacturing push is being built on an already massive industrial base.

India is already:
#2 in crude steel
#2 in cement
#2 in aluminium

One of the largest automobile producers
#2 in mobile phone production
#2 in solar PV modules

A major refining and chemicals hub
The next step is moving from scale manufacturing → technology-intensive manufacturing.

India’s Next Industrial Revolution Has Already Started. 

The next manufacturing wave is being built across:

Space → Semiconductors → Data Centers → Electronics → Solar → Aerospace

Beer is a difficult business to scale. It is heavy, expensive to transport, and taxed differently across jurisdictions, while licensing and distribution remain highly state-specific. 

That makes Asgard’s position as a large, modern and compliant brewery within the Northeast a meaningful structural advantage. 

This is not merely a geographic presence; it creates a durable commercial moat in a market where setting up and scaling capacity is difficult. 

The company already has an operating platform supporting seven owned brands, while its presence remains limited to select states. 

This leaves significant headroom to expand distribution, improve capacity utilisation and eventually add capacity as contracted demand grows.

IOL Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals Ltd. - The Ibuprofen company is slowly becoming something much bigger

👉 For years, the IOL Chemicals story was largely associated with one product: Ibuprofen. The interesting part is not simply that ibuprofen demand has recovered.
👉 It is that IOL is using its manufacturing infrastructure, backward integration and chemical capabilities to build a much broader pharmaceutical + specialty chemicals platform.
👉 IOL operates across two major businesses:
  → Pharmaceuticals / APIs
  → Chemicals

👉 The pharmaceutical business includes APIs such as:
  → Ibuprofen
  → Paracetamol
  → Metformin
  → Pantoprazole
  → Clopidogrel
 → Fenofibrate
   → Minoxidil and others

👉 The chemical business includes:
  → Ethyl Acetate
  → Iso Butyl Benzene
  → Acetic Anhydride
  → Acetyl Chloride
  → Monochloroacetic Acid
  → Triacetin
  → Other specialty/intermediate chemicals

👉 The company has total installed capacity of more than 2.1 lakh MTPA, comprising roughly 30,700 MTPA of APIs and 1.82 lakh MTPA of specialty chemicals.
👉 That gives you the first clue. IOL isn't simply a pharma company. It is a chemistry + manufacturing platform.
👉 IOL is trying to turn its Ibuprofen-led manufacturing advantage into a diversified API + specialty chemicals platform, and Q1 FY27 is one of the first quarters where that diversification is clearly visible in the numbers.

- Specialised manufacturer of hydraulic fittings including DIN Metric, JIC, ORFS, conversion and customised fittings.
- Offers 11,000+ SKUs and added 880 new SKUs in FY26.
- Serves construction, agriculture, automotive, injection moulding, railways, defence and other hydraulic applications.
- In-house forging facility provides backward integration.

FINANCIAL TRACK RECORD
- Revenue: ₹141 Cr → ₹189 Cr (FY24 → FY26)
- PAT: ₹11.6 Cr → ₹22.6 Cr
- FY26 EBITDA margin: ~24%
- PAT margin: ~12%
- ROE: ~20%
- ROCE: ~24%
- D/E: ~0.24×
- Profit growth has outpaced revenue growth, indicating potential operating leverage as the business scales.

CAPACITY RUNWAY
- Current hydraulic-fitting capacity: 483 lakh pieces/year.
- Existing utilisation:
  - Shirwal: 70.83%
  - Kavathe: 60.42%
  - Pithampur-I: 84.62%
  - Pithampur-II: 68.33%
  - Thane: 68.57%
- Expansion planned at Shirwal, Kavathe and Pithampur-I.
- Additional capacity: 187.2 lakh pieces/year.
- Post-expansion capacity: ~670 lakh pieces/year — ~39% increase.
- Key growth chain: Capacity → Utilisation → Revenue → Earnings.

FY27–FY28 REVENUE FRAMEWORK
- FY26A: ₹189 Cr
- FY27E: ₹215–230 Cr | Base case ~₹222 Cr
- FY28E: ₹250–275 Cr | Base case ~₹263 Cr
- These are estimates, not management guidance, and assume gradual capacity ramp-up and improving utilisation.

EXPORT OPPORTUNITY
- Exports were ~29% of FY26 revenue.
- USA alone contributed ~21%.
- Management/promoters have indicated an ambition to take exports toward ~50% over 1–2 years.
- Successful execution could materially expand the company's addressable market.

VALVES — FUTURE OPTIONALITY
- Company is evaluating diversification into hydraulic valves through organic and inorganic routes.
- Valves serve several of the same end markets as the existing fittings business.
- Potential evolution: Fittings → Valves → Broader Hydraulic Components Platform.
- No valuation credit should be given to future valve revenue until execution is demonstrated.

DEFENCE & RAILWAYS
- DRDO approval for supply of DIN hydraulic fittings used in defence projects.
- IRIS certification for hydraulic fittings specific to railway requirements.
- Qualifications are already in place; the opportunity is now to scale revenue from these sectors.

PEER LANDSCAPE
- Aeroflex Industries: Closest peer; FY26 revenue ~₹442 Cr, EBITDA margin ~23%, PAT ~₹55 Cr.
- Yuken India: Pumps, valves, cylinders and hydraulic systems; FY26 revenue ~₹462 Cr, EBITDA margin ~12%, PAT ~₹14 Cr.
- Dynamatic Technologies: Much larger and diversified across hydraulics, aerospace and automotive; FY26 revenue ~₹1,621 Cr.
- Hy-Tech's profitability profile is already comparable to Aeroflex despite its much smaller revenue base.

VALUATION
- Around ₹77–78/share:
  - Market cap: ~₹737 Cr
  - FY26 P/E: ~30–31×
- Valuation already reflects part of the company's profitability and growth potential.
- Key question: Can earnings grow into the valuation?

KEY RISKS
- Capacity commissioning delays
- Slow utilisation ramp-up
- Customer concentration
- Raw-material volatility
- Cyclicality
- Export execution
- Valve diversification execution
- Margin compression
- Valuation de-rating if growth disappoints

KEY TAKEAWAY
- Hy-Tech combines a small revenue base + high margins + capacity runway + export opportunity + defence/railway approvals + product diversification.
- The real thesis is whether the company can convert its ~39% capacity expansion and higher exports into sustained earnings growth.
- If execution remains strong, the Hy-Tech of FY29 could look materially different from FY26.

President Donald Trump has said U.S. economic growth could reach 20%, but that would be an extraordinary outlier by historical standards. Data going back to 1947 show that only one quarter has ever recorded annualized real GDP growth of 20% or more—the third quarter of 2020, when the economy rebounded at a 34.9% annualized rate after the pandemic shutdowns caused a historic contraction. 

The contrast with current conditions is stark: U.S. real GDP grew at just 1.5% annualized in Q2 2026. The 2020 surge was largely a rebound from an unprecedented collapse, making it a poor benchmark for normal economic expansion

GAS TURBINE SUPER CYCLE | BLADE & VANE BOTTLENECK

GE AEROSPACE — $11.75 BN CPP ACQUISITION
- GE Aerospace agreed to acquire Consolidated Precision Products (CPP) for $11.75 Bn.
- CPP is a major manufacturer of highly engineered airfoils, turbine blades/vanes and structural castings.
- GE expects its airfoil demand to rise >30% by 2030 from 2026 levels.
- CPP is expected to generate ~$2 Bn revenue in 2027.
- The deal highlights the strategic importance of precision casting capacity.

GAS TURBINE DEMAND — SUPPLY CONSTRAINED
- Siemens Energy sees sustained global gas-turbine demand of around 110–120 GW annually in the coming years.
- Siemens' gas-turbine business is effectively booked through FY2028, while 2029–30 slots are filling rapidly.
- Data centres and AI infrastructure are emerging as important demand drivers.
- The market is increasingly supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained.

AI DATA CENTRES — SPEED MATTERS
- AI data-centre power demand is creating urgency around electricity availability.
- Gas turbines can provide on-site / near-site generation, potentially reducing dependence on slower grid-infrastructure expansion.
- Faster turbine delivery is particularly valuable for hyperscaler and data-centre projects.

THE BOTTLENECK — BLADES & VANES
- Turbine manufacturing is not simply constrained by final assembly capacity.
- Precision castings, blades and vanes are among the most difficult components to manufacture at scale.
- Manufacturing requires specialised technology, high yields and deep process know-how.
- GE's CPP acquisition highlights the importance of securing this mission-critical supply chain.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR PTC / TRAC
- The major potential trigger is a new turbine-blade/vane production order from:
  - Siemens Energy
  - GE Aerospace / GE Vernova
  - Rolls-Royce
  - Safran
- A meaningful order could validate the thesis that Indian precision-casting players can become part of the global turbine supply-chain bottleneck.
- The key is not merely gas-turbine exposure, but securing qualified, long-duration blade/vane programs.

KEY TAKEAWAY
- The opportunity is shifting from “gas-turbine demand is strong” to “who can manufacture the critical components fast enough?”
- GE's $11.75 Bn CPP acquisition signals that casting capacity and manufacturing know-how are becoming strategic assets.
- For PTC / TRAC, the biggest catalyst would be new blade/vane orders from global turbine OEMs, potentially creating a meaningful change in the earnings trajectory if converted into scaled production programs.

Impact of change in EV subsidy policy from 31 July 2026

PM E-DRIVE subsidy for electric 2Ws ended on 31 Jul 2026. Govt earlier plan was to support E2W till 31 Mar 2026, then gave the industry a 4-month extension till Jul-end as there was unutilized budget

PM E-DRIVE replaced FAME-II in Oct'24 with a 10,900 Cr outlay. The idea was simple: help EV adoption scale while supporting charging infra, buses, trucks & other EV segments

initially, e-2W buyers got subsidy of 5,000/kWh, capped at 10,000/ vehicle. That was a meaningful discount for mass-market scooters. From Apr'25, cut by half to 2,500/kWh with max capped at 5,000/Veh. Signalling gradual withdrawal of support.

Now for 2W, even that 5,000 support is gone. Effective acquisition cost of an EV scooter will move up. 5,000 price hike may not sound huge, but in entry-level its imp for price-sensitive consumer

Some moderation in electric 2W demand was expected. OEMs were preparing for it as subsidy-led growth gradually transitions to product-led growth. 

August EV 2W market share came lower than July. E2W MS has come down but not in 3w as July subsidy withdrawal only 2W not in 3W. August is typically a non-festival month & seasonality also matters. OEMs should absorb subsidy via better exchange / financing offers

Market is also looking for next phase of EV support. Discussions around "FAME III" continue, but indications suggest focus could shift towards vehicle other than 2W. 2W penetration already >10% while other segment need more support

If electric 2Ws are eventually excluded from future demand subsidies, industry economics will increasingly depend on product quality, distribution, service network & battery costs instead of govt incentives.

One factor often ignored: OEMs capacity are planned in a way where capacity expansion will happen in same facility. Hence, incremental capex intensity will be far lower. Gradual drivetrain shift will continue without large incremental capex

Bottom line: Subsidy withdrawal may create short-term demand noise, but the long-term story remains the same. India's 2W market is enormous, EV penetration is still low, and the migration from ICE to EV is likely to be a long, gradual journey rather than a subsidy-driven sprint.

Avaada's proposed glass capacity is also expected to be largely captive. 
 
There is uncertainty regarding Waaree's plans to enter glass manufacturing. Given the significantly higher capital intensity of glass manufacturing, management believes entry requires substantial funding and long execution timelines. 
 
Therefore, announced industry capacity should not automatically be treated as merchant-market competition for Borosil. 
 
*9. Government policy could become a significant catalyst* 
 
Management expects government policy to remain supportive of domestic solar manufacturers. 
 
Of particular importance is the proposed *BIS/quality-control framework for solar glass*. Once the relevant standards become mandatory, management believes several overseas suppliers may no longer qualify to export glass into India. 
 
Management expects implementation around *2027*, although the government could provide an implementation window—potentially up to ~24 months—to allow domestic manufacturers to build adequate capacity. 
 
If implemented as expected, this could materially improve the competitive positioning of Indian solar-glass producers. 
 
*10. Further expansion beyond 1,600 TPD remains possible* 
 
The company has already laid infrastructure capable of supporting approximately *80 MW of power requirement for 1,600 TPD*. 
 
Management indicated that capacity could eventually be expanded towards approximately *2,800 TPD*. 
 
The economics of captive/renewable power are also attractive, with management indicating that *electricity-cost savings themselves could broadly service the associated EMI*. 
 
The company has also received the *entire government subsidy relating to its third furnace*. 
 
*Our takeaway* 
 
The meeting was encouraging. 
 
The key investment thesis is not simply rising solar demand. It is the combination of: 
 
*High entry barriers in solar glass + strong domestic demand + limited merchant domestic supply + 30–35% potential EBITDA margins + meaningful capacity addition from FY28 + possible policy protection against imports.* 
 
The immediate monitorable is the temporary SG1/SG2 maintenance shutdown and execution of the new furnaces. 
 
Beyond this, *FY28 could potentially represent a meaningful earnings inflection year* as the additional ~600 TPD capacity contributes for a full year and average production moves towards ~1,500 TPD. 
 
The biggest variables to watch remain solar-glass pricing, timing of BIS/QCO implementation, actual domestic competitor additions and execution of Borosil's capacity ramp-up to 2800 TPD.

*BOROSIL RENEWABLES – Management Interaction | Key Takeaways* 
 
Our interaction with Borosil Renewables management reinforced our view that the *solar glass industry is structurally very different from the solar module industry*, with substantially higher capital intensity, longer commissioning timelines and greater operating complexity creating meaningful entry barriers. 
 
*1. Demand outlook remains strong* 
 
Management does *not see any demand challenge* for solar glass. India is currently seeing annual solar module deployment of ~*60–65 GW*, while emerging demand from *data centres, EVs and green hydrogen* is not fully captured in this number. 
 
Management believes that even if industry demand were to fall by *20–30%*, domestic solar-glass capacity should still remain well utilised. 
 
*2. Solar glass has significantly higher entry barriers than modules* 
 
This remains one of the most important takeaways. 
 
A solar module manufacturing facility can be established with only around *₹50–100 crore/GW* of investment and can also be shut relatively quickly. 
 
Solar glass, on the other hand, requires roughly *₹300–350 crore/GW*. A *1,000 TPD glass plant requires ~₹ 2000  crore plus of investment, involves significant fuel consumption and cannot be switched on/off easily. 
 
This should structurally favour established domestic glass manufacturers as the module industry eventually consolidates. 
 
*3. Order environment remains extremely healthy* 
 
Management indicated that most monthly orders are already booked *by around the 10th of the previous month*. 
 
Importantly, demand is currently strong enough that Borosil has the ability to *choose which orders it wants to execute*, rather than chase volumes. 
 
Current solar-glass realisation is around *₹160*, with an additional surcharge of approximately *₹9.5*. 
 
Imported glass also carries the disadvantage of roughly *two months of planning/lead time* along with logistics costs. 
 
*4. 30–35% EBITDA margin indicated for glass* 
 
The glass business delivered approximately *35% EBITDA margin last quarter*. 
 
Management believes a *30–35% EBITDA margin range* is sustainable for the solar-glass business under the present operating environment. 
 
This is important because the next phase of capacity expansion can therefore translate into meaningful operating leverage if pricing remains supportive. 
 
*5. Capacity expansion starts reflecting meaningfully from FY28* 
 
Current solar-glass capacity is approximately *1,000 TPD*, with operating yields of around *69–71%*. 
 
Two additional furnaces are expected to be lit by *March 2027*, with roughly *600 TPD of incremental capacity* beginning to reflect in financial numbers from *April 2027*. 
 
Management indicated average production of around *1,500 TPD for FY28*, which suggests FY28 can be the first full year capturing the benefit of the expanded capacity. 
 
*6. Maintenance will temporarily impact production* 
 
SG1 and SG2 will undergo maintenance for approximately *75 days*. 
 
During this period, around *470 TPD* of capacity will temporarily be unavailable from the expanded ~1,600 TPD base. 
 
We would therefore distinguish between this temporary maintenance impact and the underlying demand/capacity ramp-up story. 
 
*7. Domestic capacity remains significantly short of demand* 
 
Management estimates that even after the currently planned industry expansions, domestic solar-glass manufacturing capacity would meet only around *30–40% of Indian demand*. 
 
This suggests India may continue requiring meaningful imports unless domestic capacities expand substantially. 
 
*8. Competitive capacity may be less threatening than headline announcements suggest* 
 
Management believes *Reliance's solar-glass production is likely to be consumed internally* rather than coming into the merchant market.

**CITI ON GAS CGD SECTOR | SEPTEMBER 07, 2026**

**Key Developments**
• **HP/HT Gas Allocation** – Government has revised the HP/HT gas allocation mechanism for future auctions, which should benefit larger CGDs such as **IGL & MGL**.
• **New Allocation Formula** – HP/HT gas allocation will now be linked to a CGD’s **absolute requirement**, calculated as the shortfall between **CNG + domestic PNG consumption** and its utilisation of **APM + NWG gas** in the preceding quarter.
• **Earlier Methodology** – Previously, available HP/HT gas volumes were distributed equally among eligible bidding CGDs, meaning smaller CGDs could receive the same allocation as much larger players.
• **Benefit to Large CGDs** – The revised methodology better aligns gas allocations with **actual consumption requirements**, potentially improving access to cheaper HP/HT gas for larger CGDs.
• **Margin Support** – Recent **retail price hikes by CGDs** are likely to provide additional support to margins.
• **Medium-Term Outlook** – With improved gas allocation and better pricing, the CGD sector appears well positioned from a **medium-term perspective**.

**Gas Value Chain Pecking Order**
• **MGL > IGL > GAIL > GEL > PLNG**

**Key Takeaway**
• Revised HP/HT gas allocation should structurally favour **large CGDs**, particularly **MGL & IGL**, by aligning allocations with actual gas requirements. Combined with recent retail price hikes, the changes could support **gas availability and margins**, making the sector attractive from a medium-term perspective.

**FCNR Sugar Rush What does it means for India**
FCNR experiment has turned into a blockbuster. Total inflows exceeded $136bn vs market expectations of ~$80bn. FCNR(B) deposits alone ~$127bn
  
Like Hindi movie, climax was amazing. 
Total inflows were ~$41bn by July-end, ~$73bn by Aug 21 and ~$136bn by Aug 31. Biggest forex mobilization drives India has ever seen. August was where the real frenzy happened. FCNR deposits jumped from ~$65.4bn on Aug 21 to ~$127.2bn by Aug 31.
  
Why did NRIs rush in? RBI effectively removed the pain point: currency hedging cost. Banks offered attractive yields while RBI absorbed swap costs For investors, FCNR became a rare risk-reward opportunity. Attractive $ returns + ability to leverage deposits (leverage run 4-5x)
  
FCNR nuance: Depositor takes bank credit risk but avoids INR depreciation risk since deposits remain in foreign currency. Currency mismatch is largely handled by RBI A key incentive for banks: incremental FCNR funds were exempted from CRR & SLR requirements.
  
More deployable money, less regulatory drag hence higher NIMs, Every $ mobilized can potentially earn better spreads for banks Flip side: Liquidity is now overflowing. System liquidity has surged sharply as these inflows entered the banking system

When banks are flush with money, appetite for wholesale funding drops. That's already showing up in lower CD rates & softer short-term funding costs Excess liquidity usually pushes overnight money market rates lower. Too much cash chasing too few opportunities compress yields
 
The RBI also gets a strategic advantage. Larger forex reserves and dollar balances improve its ability to manage forward market positions & reduce pressure from speculative USD demand. Forward dollar short should be reduced going forward
 
For currency speculator, the message is important. Betting aggressively against ₹ becomes tougher when RBI has significantly larger forex ammunition and stronger external buffers Now comes the hard part. Raising $136bn is the easy part.
  
Deploying it productively is the challenge. These are time-bound liabilities with an embedded cost. Eventually the money must earn more than it costs. INR already showing strength: USDINR below 95 today
 
The success of this scheme won't be judged by the $136bn raised. It will be judged by whether India converts this liquidity windfall into stronger growth, stable ₹, lower funding stress & productive credit creation over the next few years

Good Bad & Ugly Side of Happiest Mind / ITC infotech merger Happiest Minds is merging into ITC Infotech. Promoters led by Ashok Soota will first sell a 22.1% stake to ITC for ~₹1,330 Cr at ₹390-400/share (1330cr for 22%), followed by the merger

Is Pvt Banks Really Losing Share vs PSU Banks?

Everyone is talking about PSU banks taking share from Pvt banks. The narrative is simple: PSU banks are growing faster than Pvt banks, so PSU banks are winning. But the reality is a lot more nuanced.

Argument is : PSU banks are fine with 1.0-1.3% RoA vs  Pvt banks target higher profitability. Pvt banks don't want to trade-off profitability for growth.

This has impacted valuations. Premium Pvt bank multiples came with expectation of steadily MS gain vs PSU. Post-Covid, that trend has slowed, creating doubts.

If PSU banks are sacrificing yield for growth, where should it show up first? HFC, safest retail assets with low NPA, Yet PSU bank share has drifted from ~35% in FY21 to ~34% in H1FY26, while Pvt banks have inched up from ~39% to ~40%.

If PSU banks were aggressively chasing growth regardless of return, housing should have been the biggest battleground. The data doesn't show that. PSU gained initially, now plateaued. 

PSU not gainin share from Pvt banks. Market share remained stable, data also inc. HDFC merger boost for pvt bank

So where is PSU growth actually coming from? A large part is Gold Loans.

Many Pvt banks have stayed away from becoming aggressive gold lenders. The business is operationally intensive and risky. PSU banks have been far more active, esp Canara/SBIN. 

Recently, incremental industry gold loan growth has come primarily from PSU banks, increasing their dominance in banking gold-loan AUM.

Second area is Agri lending. PSU banks have stepped up agri lending. May be it’s mandate-driven, or due to deeper reach into semi-urban and rural India where Agri credit demand is.
These segments Pvt banks is not that agressive. PSU banks are gaining share at the system level. But pvt dominance continue in safe mortgages, affluent retail.

Jefferies power equipment

Many Problem: Solar led grid instability / Energy import / Pollution One solution: EV India is winning solar race. Solar supply a huge chunk of daytime power, pushing net grid demand sharply lower arnd noon. But demand peaks after sunset. That's the classic "duck curve" problem

~80 GW swing created largely by renewable output. The irony: clean power is available when demand isn't. Several states doing solar curtailment as the grid couldn't absorb all midday generation. So, next phase of green transition is tougher than just adding more solar panels

India imports ~90% of its crude oil needs & roughly half of its natural gas . Energy security remains one of the biggest economic vulnerabilities. Crude oil is among India's largest import items. Every $ oil prices widens the import bill = trade deficit = pressure on Rupee

Air pollution remains a public health emergency in major metros. Delhi frequently records PM2.5 levels many multiples above WHO norms, while Mumbai too has seen worsening air quality episodes. Solar, oil imports & air pollution are not separate challenges. They are connected

The common link is urban transport. A large share of oil consumption in metros comes from ICE cars commuting daily between home & office. Think about office parking lots. Vehicles remain parked for 8-10 hrs during the exact period when solar generation is highest

What if every major office complex became a daytime EV charging hub? Cars would consume power when solar generation is abundant, helping flatten the duck curve instead of deepening it.

Corp can accelerate this shift. EV subsidy for employees & workplace chargin infra can become part of CSR spend (2% of PBT) Vehicles in metros spend most working hours parked at offices. Converting 20%+ of parking capacity into chargers can create a daytime demand for solar power

One solution. Multiple benefits. More EVs = lower oil imports, cleaner city air, higher daytime power consumption, better solar utilisation & stable grid. Sometimes the smartest energy storage isn't a battery plant. It's millions of parked EVs connected to chargers.

Underappreciated SBI MF's distribution moat 

SBI MF's biggest advantage isn't fund performance. It's distribution. In India, bank-backed AMCs blessed with an edge as the bank branch is still the most powerful financial distribution channel
Investors trust banks with savings, salaries & FDs. Convincing a depositor to buy a bank-sponsored MF is far easier than acquiring a customer from scratch. Trust compounds over time
This trust factor is visible across the industry. 4 of India's top 5 AMCs are bank-backed. Even with rising competition, large AMCs have largely retained market share
SBI has the widest reach across the country, with one of the largest branch networks, customer bases & geographic presence among all financial institutions. That reach is difficult to replicate
Unlike most AMCs, SBI MF gets disproportionate support from its parent. SBI Bank contributes 35% of SBI MF's equity AUM. Compare that with just 8% for ICICI AMC & 6% for HDFC AMC
More interestingly, 40% of SBI MF's equity AUM comes through bank channels, versus 19% for ICICI AMC & 12% for HDFC AMC. SBI's distribution engine remains a major growth driver
Most banks operate open architecture & recommend products across AMCs based on suitability. SBI may have open architecture formally, but data suggests SBI customers get mostly SBI-branded investment products
The numbers are striking. 100% of SBI MF's promoter-bank sourced AUM sits with SBI, vs 70% for ICICI AMC & just 28% for HDFC AMC. That's about as captive as distribution gets
SBI's MF penetration opportunity is still huge. Average MF AUM per SBI branch is only ~10% of retail deposits per branch, implying a long runway for existing customers to migrate from deposits into MFs
The next leg of growth likely comes from B30 markets. SBI MF already has the highest B30 equity AUM share at 16%, ahead of ICICI AMC (12%) & HDFC AMC (11%)
SBI's deep Tier-2/Tier-3 presence matters. 66% of SBI MF's SIPs originate from B30 markets, giving it access to underpenetrated investors who are just beginning their financialization journey
The final edge is economics. SBI MF's distribution cost through SBI is just 65 bps, lower than HDFC AMC's 68 bps & ICICI AMC's 69 bps. Better reach + higher trust + lower cost = a distribution moat that's hard to disrupt

The Relationship Trump Misunderstood:
For three decades, China and emerging markets effectively exported disinflation to the developed world. They produced goods at a fraction of Western costs and shipped them to consumers in the US and Europe. The result: lower prices and higher purchasing power
The West got cheaper TVs, phones, clothes, furniture and industrial goods. China got manufacturing jobs, export growth and rising incomes. It wasn't a one-way relationship. Both sides benefited
As exports surged, China accumulated enormous foreign exchange reserves. Every dollar earned from exports added to a growing pool of savings that had to be invested somewhere
Those reserves served two purposes: protect the yuan from volatility and build strategic national wealth. China used them to buy foreign assets, resources, companies and financial securities around the world
A large portion of those reserves found their way into US Treasuries. China became one of the largest lenders to the US government, recycling export earnings back into America's financial system
This mattered because sustained Treasury demand helped keep long-term US interest rates lower than they otherwise would have been. Cheap imports lowered inflation. Treasury purchases lowered financing costs
In effect, China was helping on two fronts: suppressing goods inflation through low-cost manufacturing and supporting bond markets through reserve recycling. 
Trump focused heavily on one side of the equation: the trade deficit. From that perspective, China was exporting too much and manufacturing jobs were leaving America. This became the basis for tariffs and trade confrontation.
But the other side received less attention. Those same imports were keeping prices low for US consumers. Many products became affordable precisely because they were manufactured in lower-cost economies
The relationship also extended to capital markets. China's reserve accumulation created a steady source of demand for US government bonds, helping support the broader financial system
Today that world is changing. China is no longer a low-income economy desperate for export growth. Wages have risen, technology has improved and its economic influence is far greater than it was 20 years ago
The old model of unlimited cheap labour, ever-rising globalization and automatic reserve recycling is fading. Both countries increasingly view the relationship through a strategic lens rather than purely an economic one
As supply chains fragment and tariffs rise, the US may face more inflation from its own policy choices. Producing goods domestically or through alternative supply chains is often more resilient, but rarely cheaper
At the same time, if foreign demand for Treasuries becomes less predictable, bond investors may demand higher yields to absorb increasing government debt. Higher yields mean higher financing costs across the economy
The next decade may look very different from the last three. Less globalization, more strategic competition, potentially higher inflation and structurally higher interest rates. Markets are still figuring out what that world looks like
Bottom line: The US-China relationship wasn't simply buyer vs seller. It was a system where goods, capital and inflation dynamics were deeply intertwined. Breaking that system may create consequences on both sides.
